What are the harf al-jars that we learned so far? Fi means in, ala means on, ila means to, min means from, and li means for or belongs to. We reviewed that female names do not take tanween, e.g., Zaynabu and Fatimatu, and learned that ayna belongs to adawat al-istifham and is used to ask about place. We reviewed huwa and hiya as third-person pronouns, with huwa for singular masculine and hiya for singular feminine or feminine objects. The class translated example sentences using fi and ala and reviewed vocabulary such as talib, masjid, ghurfa, qalam, mirhad, and hammam. We learned that generally nouns without al take tanween except for exceptions such as female names and mudaf constructions. We introduced two new harf al-jars, ila and min, and translated sentences like ana min al-yabani and huwa min al-sin. We learned the first verbs in the class, kharaja and dhahaba, and discussed that Arabic words are divided into ism, fi'l, and harf. Verbs indicate action and tense, and kharaja tells us past tense, masculine, singular, and third person. We compared forms like kharaja, kharajaa, kharajoo, kharajta, and kharajtu and emphasized identifying the fa'il when translating. We then moved to lesson five and reviewed mudaf and mudaf ilayh as a 'blank of blank' construction, such as kitab-u Muhammadin and qalam-u Hamidin. Rules discussed included: the mudaf comes first, the mudaf does not take al or tanween, the mudaf ilayh generally takes kasra, nothing comes between mudaf and mudaf ilayh, and the mudaf does not have to be marfu'. Exceptions were mentioned such as Musa and man, which do not change form, and ghayr al-munsarif examples like Ibrahima عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام which take fathah instead of kasrah. We reviewed harf al-nida ya, which is used for calling someone and causes the following noun to take one dhammah without tanween, e.g., ya Yasiru and ya Allah. We learned hadhihi as the feminine counterpart to hadha and reviewed gender agreement in adjectives such as waqifatun for feminine and jalisun for masculine. Hamzat al-wasl was introduced, explaining that it is pronounced at the beginning of speech but dropped in connected speech, unlike hamzat al-qat'. Vocabulary such as aydan, muhandisat, tabibat, sayyarah, and liman was introduced, along with the rule that lam causes kasrah, as in lillahi. We learned that jiddan always has fathah and means 'very'. Exceptions to feminine nouns were covered, including words that are feminine despite lacking ta marbutah, such as shams, nar, jahannam, dunya, qidr, sabil, tariq, and nafs. Finally, we learned that body parts with pairs, such as yad, ayn, and rijl, are generally feminine, while body parts without pairs are masculine. The session ended with discussion of the upcoming test, possible question formats, and a review session after the break.
title: Arabic Grammar: حُرُوف الْجَرّ (ḥurūf al-jarr : prepositions), مُضَاف (muḍāf : possessed noun) and مُضَافٌ إِلَيْهِ (muḍāf ilayhi : possessor), Verbs in فِعْل مَاضِي (fiʿl māḍī : past tense)
summary: The session covered advanced grammar topics including the functions and usage of حُرُوف الْجَرّ (ḥurūf al-jarr : prepositions — making following words مَجْرُور — majrūr : genitive), rules governing مُضَاف (muḍāf : possessed noun) and مُضَافٌ إِلَيْهِ (muḍāf ilayhi : possessor), and فِعْل مَاضِي (fiʿl māḍī : past tense) verbs indicating مُذَكَّر (mudhakkar : masculine), مُفْرَد (mufrad : singular), third person. Key examples included فِي (fī : in), عَلَى (ʿalā : on) as prepositions and verbs like خَرَجَ (kharaja : he exited) for actions in the past.
key_points: حُرُوف الْجَرّ (ḥurūf al-jarr — e.g., فِي — fī : in, عَلَى — ʿalā : on, إِلَى — ilā : to, مِنْ — min : from, لِـ — li- : for) make the following word مَجْرُور (majrūr : genitive — typically with كَسْرَة). Example: فِي الْمَسْجِدِ (fī l-masjidi : in the mosque).

أَسْمَاء الْمُؤَنَّث (asmāʾ al-muʾannath : feminine proper names) do not take تَنْوِين (tanwīn — e.g., فَاطِمَةُ، زَيْنَبُ، مَرْيَمُ), unlike regular مُؤَنَّث (muʾannath : feminine) nouns which may still take تَنْوِين (e.g., سَاعَةٌ — sāʿatun : a watch).

فِعْل مَاضِي (fiʿl māḍī : past tense verb — e.g., خَرَجَ — kharaja : he exited, ذَهَبَ — dhahaba : he went) indicates four things in this form: مَاضِي (māḍī : past tense), مُذَكَّر (mudhakkar : masculine), مُفْرَد (mufrad : singular), and third person.

مُضَاف (muḍāf : possessed noun) and مُضَافٌ إِلَيْهِ (muḍāf ilayhi : possessor) construction is translated as 'the X of Y' (e.g., كِتَابُ مُحَمَّدٍ — kitābu muḥammadin : the book of Muḥammad). Rules: the مُضَاف (muḍāf) comes first, cannot have اَلْ or تَنْوِين, the مُضَافٌ إِلَيْهِ (muḍāf ilayhi) is generally مَجْرُور (majrūr : genitive), and nothing comes between them.
ظَرْف (ẓarf : adverb of place or time) words indicate place or time (e.g., هُنَاكَ — hunāka : there, تَحْتَ — taḥta : under) and are used to describe location or timing.

حَرْف النِّدَاء (ḥarf al-nidāʾ : the vocative particle) يَا (yā : O) is used to call someone and generally makes the following noun take a single ضَمَّة (ḍammah) without تَنْوِين (e.g., يَا يَاسِرُ، يَا اللَّهُ).

Demonstrative pronouns: هَٰذَا (hādhā : this [masc. sg. near]) is used for مُذَكَّر (mudhakkar : masculine) singular nearby objects, while هَٰذِهِ (hādhihi : this [fem. sg. near]) is used for مُؤَنَّث (muʾannath : feminine) singular nearby objects.

Words describing مُؤَنَّث (muʾannath : feminine) nouns take تَاء مَرْبُوطَة (tāʾ marbūṭah : the feminine marker ة), such as وَاقِفَةٌ (wāqifatun : standing [fem.]) and مُهَنْدِسَةٌ (muhandisatun : female engineer).

Some nouns are مُؤَنَّث (muʾannath : feminine) despite lacking تَاء مَرْبُوطَة (tāʾ marbūṭah) and must be memorized (e.g., شَمْسٌ — shamsun : sun, نَارٌ — nārun : fire, جَهَنَّمُ — jahannam : hellfire, نَفْسٌ — nafsun : soul, سَبِيلٌ — sabīlun : path).

General body-part gender rule: body parts with one counterpart are typically مُذَكَّر (mudhakkar : masculine), while body parts with two counterparts (e.g., يَدٌ — yadun : hand, عَيْنٌ — ʿaynun : eye, رِجْلٌ — rijlun : foot) are generally مُؤَنَّث (muʾannath : feminine).
questions: [00:49:01] Q: How are body parts grammatically categorized? — A: Body parts with counterparts (arms, eyes) are مُؤَنَّث (muʾannath : feminine); those without pairs like the nose are مُذَكَّر (mudhakkar : masculine).

[00:23:00] Q: Why is the مُضَافٌ إِلَيْهِ (muḍāf ilayhi : possessor) sometimes not in كَسْرَة (kasrah)? — A: Exceptions include names that are غَيْرُ الْمُنْصَرِف (ghayr al-munṣarif : diptote) such as مُوسَى (Mūsā) and إِبْرَاهِيمَ (Ibrāhīma) which take فَتْحَة (fatḥah) instead of كَسْرَة.
